system.name: Universal Scene Graph (USG)
system.one_liner: One scene-graph representation that can be generated from any combination of text, image, video and 3D point-cloud input, merging what each single-modality graph offers.

content.variant_note: four single-modality scene graphs in coloured cards over their raw inputs, contrasted with one universal graph band below
content.argues: Scene graphs of single modalities each describe the same scene with different strengths; the universal graph keeps all of them and marks which modality each object came from.
content.subject: One scene (a person with headphones on a sofa with a phone) as a sentence, image, video and point cloud, each with its scene graph, and the merged universal graphs.

lessons.what_to_learn: To show a unification, draw the same instance once per source in one visual grammar with its own coloured header and an arrow from its raw input, then merge them in one wide band below whose items carry small colour stamps for their source. Keep item colours fixed across all graphs.
lessons.suits: Papers that unify several modalities, views or data sources into one representation and want to show what each source adds.

evidence: Caption: single-modality scene graphs for text, image, video and 3D at the top, the proposed Universal SG at the bottom.
Caption: the shown USG uses all four modalities, but any modality can be absent.
Section 2: the textual object Peter corresponds to the visual object person, and the 3D sofa to the image sofa.

summary: Universal Scene Graph Generation proposes one scene-graph representation that can be built from any mix of text, image, video and 3D input. Figure 1 uses one scene, a person with headphones relaxing on a sofa with a phone. Four tinted cards at the top show what a scene graph of each single modality looks like: a sentence graph, an image graph, a sequence of video graphs on skewed planes and a 3D graph. Each card sits over its raw input and is joined to it by a colour-matched arrow. A pink band at the bottom holds five consecutive universal graphs whose nodes carry tiny colour stamps naming their source modality, explained by a key. Object colours stay the same in every graph.
